summary: For ages 7–9: name and locate the five named oceans (Pacific — largest and deepest; Atlantic; Indian; Southern — ringing Antarctica; Arctic — smallest and coldest) on both a flat map and a globe, and understand that they are one continuous body of salt water divided into named basins by people for convenience. The central conceptual insight is 'five names, one ocean', with the recently recognised Southern Ocean as a concrete example that geographic conventions change over time.
misconceptions: 'The oceans are separate, walled-off seas' — not grasping they form one continuous global ocean.
'There have always been exactly five oceans' — unaware the count/boundaries are human conventions that changed (Southern Ocean recognised recently).
Confusing 'ocean' with 'sea' (a sea is a smaller region within/adjoining an ocean).
Mislocating oceans — e.g. placing the Indian Ocean or swapping Atlantic/Pacific on the map.
Thinking the Arctic 'isn't a real ocean' because it's frozen — sea ice sits on ocean water.

activities.title: Trace the unbroken water: five names, one ocean
steps: On a globe (physical spinnable globe or a rotatable digital globe), start in the Pacific and trace one finger along the water: round the bottom of the world through the Southern Ocean, up into the Atlantic and north into the Arctic, then back down the Atlantic, round the southern tip of Africa and across into the Indian — without ever lifting off water.
Say aloud the name of each ocean as you pass into it.
Compare with a flat world map and notice how the edges of the flat map hide the fact that the water wraps around and joins up.
State in your own words why the trace proves the oceans are 'one ocean with five names'.
activities.insight: The five named oceans are a single connected body of salt water; the names and boundaries are human conventions, not physical walls. A globe reveals the connectedness that a flat map's edges disguise.

activities.title: Name and place the five oceans
steps: On a blank or unlabelled world map, place or write each of the five ocean names in the correct basin: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, Arctic.
Repeat the placement several times across the session (not once) until you can place at least three reliably, then all five.
Attach a memory hook to each: Pacific = biggest, Arctic = smallest and partly covered by floating sea ice at the top, Southern = rings Antarctica at the bottom, plus Atlantic and Indian between them.
Check your placement against a labelled reference map and correct any swaps.
activities.insight: Reliable location memory comes from repeated active placement and self-correction, anchored by a memorable fact for each ocean.

activities.title: Would the dye reach the other ocean? (reasoning check)
steps: Answer the travel question: if a drop of dye (or a fish) started in the middle of the Pacific, could it ever reach the Atlantic without leaving the water? Explain how.
Decide true or false: 'the oceans are separate seas walled off from each other by land', and justify your choice.
Identify which ocean is largest and which is coldest, and find the coldest one on a globe (at the very top, around the North Pole, where much of the water is covered by floating sea ice).
Explain why people gave one connected ocean five different names.
activities.insight: A learner who holds the connected-ocean concept can justify that water (and a fish) can travel between any oceans, because the basins join around the continents; naming is for human convenience.

activities.title: The newest ocean: conventions change
steps: Compare a 'four oceans' view (historic) with a 'five oceans' view (Southern Ocean added) — for example via a toggle or two reference maps.
Discuss the question: if the water around Antarctica was always there, what actually changed when the Southern Ocean was named?
Explain in your own words that the count and boundaries of oceans are human conventions that have changed over time.
activities.insight: Geographic conventions evolve: the Southern Ocean being recognised recently shows that the number of named oceans is a human decision, not a change in the water itself.

checkQuestion: On a globe I point to the Pacific, the Atlantic and the Indian oceans, each with its own name and colour on the map. A child says 'so the oceans are separate seas with walls of land between them'. Do you agree — and if a fish could swim wherever it liked, could it get from one ocean to another without ever leaving the water?
checkAnswer: The named oceans are really one connected body of salt water — a single global ocean divided up and named by people for convenience. A fish (or a drop of water) could travel from the Pacific to the Atlantic to the Indian and round to the Southern and Arctic without ever leaving the water, because they all join up around the continents. The five named oceans are Pacific (biggest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern (round Antarctica) and Arctic (smallest and coldest).
